utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I understand you intend to open the case for the Defence of Mr. Lazarevic with a short opening statement. Please proceed with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. Your Honours, General Lazarevic's Defence, in its oral arguments presented in accordance with Rule 98 bis, argued and provided evidence in support of the position that the Prosecution had failed to prove that General Lazarevic was criminally responsible for the perpetration of the alleged crimes listed in paragraphs 1 through 5 of the indictment, either under Article 7(1) or under Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. As opposed to the standard that was applied by the Trial Chamber in giving weight to the evidence submitted under Rule 98 bis, which is lower than the standard "beyond reasonable doubt," General Lazarevic's Defence is convinced that the documents and witnesses it intends to call in this case will convince the Trial Chamber that there is more than reasonable doubt about General Lazarevic's criminal responsibility for the crimes he's charged with under the indictment. The Defence -- the Prosecution claims that General Lazarevic participated in a joint criminal enterprise aimed at changing the ethnic balance in Kosovo in an effort to ensure permanent Serbian control over the province. The Defence will prove that there was no plan to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo, and ipso facto there was no joint criminal enterprise in which the accused Lazarevic was supposed to have participated. The Prosecution wants to suggest that the accused Lazarevic, as a member of the so-called "Joint Command," commanded, controlled, directed or had effective control in other ways over the Pristina Corps and the forces subordinate to it, and these forces took part in the commission of the crimes that the accused are charged with in this indictment. The Defence will present a number of documents and call a number of witnesses to prove that the single chain of command in the Army of Yugoslavia was not disrupted at any point by the existence of any parallel or any other kind of command in which the accused Lazarevic purportedly participated outside of the chain of command that was envisaged and established in accordance with the law. The Defence will further prove that General Lazarevic exerted command exclusively over the forces of the Pristina Corps that was replenished by the troops from the Army of Yugoslavia that were resubordinated to it in a legitimate and lawful way pursuant to the orders issued by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia or, rather, the Supreme Command Staff and the 3rd Army Command. General Lazarevic never commanded or had effective control over the units of the Ministry of the Interior or the units of the civilian defence and the civilian protection that were subordinated directly to the Ministry of Defence. There is ample evidence and there are numerous witnesses to show that the MUP units were never resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. Furthermore, volunteers joined the Pristina Corps units or they were received in the Pristina Corps units at a higher level of command in a manner that was strictly stipulated by the law. There is ample documentary evidence and word-of-mouth testimony that will confirm that the accused Lazarevic, as the corps commander, ordered additional measures to check the volunteers that were sent to the corps by the superior command. In the indictment, General Lazarevic is charged with planning, instigating and ordering operations and activities of the Pristina Corps and the forces subordinated to it that took part in the commission of the crimes that the accused are charged with in this indictment. Lazarevic is further charged with having personally directed those operations. The Trial Chamber will see ample evidence to support the claim that General Lazarevic never took part in the planning and instigation of actions or operations targeting the civilian population. In fact, he never issued any written or oral orders to that purpose or to that effect. Quite the contrary. There is ample evidence to show that General Lazarevic issued orders, took measures, and even set up special task forces to receive, assist and take care of the civilian population that happened to be in the combat zone or who were endangered by NATO air strikes. We will tender a lot of documents, call a lot of evidence, to show that the accused Lazarevic, as the corps commander, demanded from his subordinate units to comply with the Laws and Customs of War the Geneva Conventions, and the Rules of International Humanitarian Law. General Lazarevic was not in control of operations in which crimes were allegedly committed, and the Defence will particularly seek to prove the untruthfulness of the testimony of witness Nike Peraj to the effect that the accused Lazarevic personally was in control of the operation in Meja and Korenica, as he put it, on the 27th, 28th and 29th of April, 1999. There are numerous written proofs and witnesses who will corroborate that on the stated dates, General Lazarevic simply was not in Djakovica. Neither can the accused Lazarevic shoulder responsibility -- criminal responsibility on the basis of aiding and abetting any possible crimes, because he was not aware of the existence of any criminal plan targeting the civilian Albanian population in Kosovo and Metohija in the period relevant for this indictment. There is also ample evidence that shows without any doubt that the accused Lazarevic was not aware of the existence of any criminal plan targeting ethnic Albanians. After all, that can be clearly and unambiguously concluded from his orders and other documents which we will be presenting to the Trial Chamber. Equally ungrounded are the allegations in the indictment to the effect that the accused Lazarevic tolerated the commission of crimes and participated in the planning, instigation and ordering of concealment of crimes. On the contrary, the accused Lazarevic insisted, within the bounds of his powers, that the corps organs within whose competence this was undertake every preventative measure, as well as for the perpetrators of all types of criminal offences to be investigated, detected and put on trial. At this point, the claim that the accused Lazarevic was not aware of the existence of a criminal plan may sound contradictory, seeing that on the other side he undertook prevention measures to prevent the commission of criminal offences and measures for the detection and trying of the perpetrators. We should like to mention before this august Trial Chamber that in the period relevant for this indictment, there was a war raging in Kosovo and Metohija, and that in every war there exist individuals who are prepared to take advantage of the chaotic situation which war entails as such, to commit criminal offences. It is, hence, clear that these were isolated incidents perpetrated by individuals and not willful and systematic action within the commission of a criminal enterprise, as claimed by the Prosecution. Finally, the Defence will offer to the Trial Chamber ample evidence to prove that General Lazarevic took the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of criminal offences and punish the perpetrators, ample evidence about the return of volunteers, the filing of criminal charges both against officers as well as men, perpetrators of criminal offences, and the preventative informing and warning of subordinated units that in conditions of the war conflict which was obtaining in the period which is relevant for this indictment, they had to strictly abide by the provisions of International Humanitarian Law and the Laws and Customs of War shall indubitably demonstrate that the accused Lazarevic is not criminally responsible either under Article 7(1) or Article 7(3) of the Statute for the offences which he is charged with in the indictment. One of the Defence witnesses of General Ojdanic, General Kosovac, stated before the Trial Chamber that General Lazarevic, after the Kumanovo Agreement had been reached, left the province only after his last soldier had left Kosovo. It is in that spirit that he has decided to take the stand before this august Trial Chamber as the first witness before his subordinated commanders and soldiers. Your Honours, the Defence of General Lazarevic calls its first witness, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Lazarevic, could you make your way, please, to the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while he's coming down, I'd just like to introduce a new face on our Prosecution team. This is Mr. Manoj Sachdeva who will be appearing in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, will you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will now tell you something you have heard here many times before, but I would like you to bear in mind that we speak the same language and to wait for the interpretation in order not to have to intervene because of errors in the transcript. May we start? General, in the indictment there is some information -- there are some details, but for the record please tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Lazarevic. I was born on the 23rd of March, 1949, in the municipality of Babusnica in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, how long was your military career?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-two years of effective professional military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Throughout these 32 years of an effective military career, what duties did you perform in the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Numerous duties, primarily command duties, from the lowest tactical level, from platoon commander, up to the strategic commander, army commander, and deputy chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We will now focus on the period relevant for the indictment in order not to waste time speaking about the start of your military career. How and in what manner were you appointed to your duty in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I wish to say that in 1996 and 1997, I held the duty of chief of Staff of the Nis Corps of the 3rd Army with its headquarters in Nis. On the 31st of December, 1997, I received an oral order from the commander of the Nis Corps that on the same day, on New Year's Eve, I should go to Pristina and take up a new duty. When I asked him why this was so sudden, because he told me about this at 6.30 in the morning, he explained to me that this was a decision by the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Perisic. Let me add, I went to the Pristina garrison within a few days to take up my new duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we will now document what you have just said, and I need an explanation concerning two exhibits. Could we have on e-court Exhibit 5D1323. Your Honours, while we are waiting for this exhibit, these are documents from the personnel file. They are on the mandated list, and I can say that at the very outset, many documents have not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's on the amended list, interpret's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 90 per cent of these documents have not yet been translated, the ones we will use initially, and I hope this will not discourage the Court. I see my learned friend on his feet, and I would like to know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to address the question first, but it does discourage the Prosecution that we don't have English translations of a number of documents. By my rough count, there were approximately 700 exhibits listed to be tendered through this witness, and I'm only about three quarters of the way through reviewing those. Up to this point, I've noted some 138 for which there are no translations. It makes it very difficult for me to know how to prepare and how to deal with this. I just want to put that objection on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Bakrac, has anything changed since immediately following the meeting that took place about translation difficulties? My impression was that most translation would be resolved before your defence started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have -- or rather as my learned friend said, the exhibits we wish to tender through this witness are on our priority list, and what I can say is that we have received translations of almost 90 per cent of the documents we wish to open in e-court. As for the remaining documents we wish to tender, there may be a larger proportion of untranslated ones, but we can mark these with an IC number and when the translation arrives the Prosecution will have an opportunity to object to the admission of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm somewhat confused. You told us a little while ago that 90 per cent of the documents had not yet -- I thought you said "translated," "been translated", but the transcript says "used initially." You did say "translated"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now you say 90 per cent have been translated, and I'm somewhat confused by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there may be a misunderstanding concerning the interpretation. I said 90 per cent of the documents we intend to open in e-court with this witness have already been translated, and I said I thought there would be no difficulty concerning these. We will tender the remaining documents, and they can be marked with an IC number until the Prosecution sees the translation and has an opportunity to object, to object to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clarified the translation issue and the misinterpretation. Mr. Hannis, it looks as though it's a question of specific relief as and when required, rather than any other measure at this stage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it may be, Your Honour. May I add some additional information explaining my position? The original notification I got for this witness, by my rough count, there were 697 exhibits. I have not been able to go through the entire list, but among the first 486 exhibits, there were 138 for which there were no translations. There were an additional 53 which appeared in e-court that there were translations, but when I tried to access them, I had the red letter notification "denied." Now, I hope those have been released to the Prosecution at this point, but as of Monday, I think that was the case. So there were some 191 out of 486. Now, Mr. Bakrac says 90 per cent of the ones he's going to use have been translated, so maybe he's using some significantly smaller number than 697, but as you say, maybe it's -- I'm going to have to raise it as they come. And this first one, I see I don't have a translation for. It appears to be just an appointment, and that's not such a difficulty for me. But once we get into 1998 and 1999 and combat orders and other things, it will be a bigger problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Bakrac, we'll deal with these problems when they arise, so please proceed with this one, which will be, as in the case of all untranslated documents, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This first document has not been translated. General -- may it be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in e-court before you is an order. It's order number 10-196, dated the 30th of December, 1997. What sort of order is this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. At that time, that was General Perisic, concerning my transfer from the Nis garrison to the Pristina garrison. I wish to point out that the first time I saw this order was a few months ago. I repeat, I acted on oral orders when I carried out this task and went to take up my new duty. A few months ago, my Defence asked my personnel -- asked for my personnel file from the army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Serbia, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on e-court Exhibit 5D1324.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note, Your Honour, this is another one for which we have no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just about to say that we have no translation for this document. May it please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, this is an order dated the 12th of January, issued also by General Perisic. It appears to be identical to the previous one. Can you explain what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The two orders are different. The first one concerns my transfer from one garrison to another, from one unit to another. This is a specific order issued by the chief of the General Staff, appointing me to the establishment duty of chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps. That is a duty with the establishment element of colonel-general, and the chief of the General Staff, by this order, appointed me to the duty of colonel. According to the establishment elements, that is the same duty I had held for the previous two years in the Nis Corps of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when did you take up your duty as chief of the Staff of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I took up that duty on the 9th of January, 1998, as is evident from this order, although it's dated the 12th of January. In the last sentence, it says that the appointment holds good from the date the 9th of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be a bit early in the day to make this intervention, but I think I should before we get bogged down. At first glance, this looks like a complete and utter waste of time, Mr. Bakrac. I don't think there's any issue over the fact, which is in the indictment, that Mr. Lazarevic was appointed in 1998, and we're now learning at the beginning of 1998, to the position of chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps. Now, it may be that it's important, personally, to get it absolutely cut and dried, "I"s dotted and the "T"s crossed, but this is a battle that doesn't exist in this case. Let's make progress rapidly to things that matter that are in issue, and let's not get bogged down in documents that we really don't need to see, which have caused a debate that probably took five minutes of our time and was pointless. Can we just get straight into the case? Otherwise, you'll be -- you'll run out of time on things that don't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please hear me out. There is an explanation for this. The Prosecutor, I can't recall precisely whether in his opening statement or in his 98 bis submission, said that General Lazarevic was Milosevic's choice. We feel this is important in order to demonstrate who brought General Lazarevic to the post of chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, so this is not mere information to the Chamber as to how he arrived there, but we wish to show that it was six months after that that he was appointed by an ordinance at the proposal of General Perisic. So those were the reasons why we presented these documents and this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the existing evidence, Mr. Bakrac, that General Lazarevic was Milosevic's personal choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend, Mr. Hannis, I assume deducted this from the fact that General Lazarevic was appointed in December by an ordinance of President Milosevic, as commander of the Pristina Corps, so we wanted to present evidence challenging this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there evidence of such an ordinance or are you telling me that you're relying for this on Mr. Hannis' say so, which is not evidence in the case, as you know. Sorry, maybe I'm misunderstanding the significance of something, but it doesn't look like an issue to me, so please move on to something that may be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even if he was Milosevic's personal choice, I'm absolutely certain you'd find a document through the normal command structure that appointed him anyway, Mr. Bakrac. That's not going to help us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we have heard before this Tribunal and the indictment also mentions that you were promoted twice in Mr. Milosevic's time. Had you been promoted before that and after that period, the period that is when Mr. Kostunica was president?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In my 32 years of effective military career, I was promoted before the usual time, five times. In the time of the former Yugoslavia, in Tito's time, under the presidency of the then Yugoslavia, I was promoted twice under Mr. Milosevic's [as interpreted] President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia I was also promoted to the rank of colonel by an ordinance of -- and then I was also promoted by an ordinance of President Kostunica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to put another question to you, and for the sake of the Trial Chamber I will say it refers to paragraph 5 of the indictment, which says that you were commended officially on two occasions for your role, and we have also heard the testimony of Nike Peraj, who said that after the action in Korenica, in Meja, you were commended. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely not correct, and this can all be checked in my personnel file, because incentives for professional members of the army are always entered into the personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to correct the interpretation on page 15, line 7, where it says that he was promoted to his highest rank by President Milosevic, whereas the witness said he had been promoted by President Kostunica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your point, Mr. Bakrac. I was also thinking just now of the evidence of Mr. Radinovic, who spoke of the role of the chief of the General Staff as simply the person who executed decisions that were made by the supreme commander, so I suppose there was evidence on which Mr. Hannis may be able to rely to suggest that there is personal choice of Lazarevic by the president. So I was probably wrong to intervene in that way, and indeed the very fact that Perisic does execute the order of appointment would, on that basis, rather support the view that he was the personal choice of Milosevic. And what's just been said about appointment or promotion by Kostunica would tend to confirm that, that the president is the person who actually makes the appointments at that level, although that's something we would need to look at all the evidence on, including what was said by Radinovic. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just ask one more additional question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On whose proposal are such decisions on appointment made by the president?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia is authorised to propose to the president of the state such things for the army personnel, and as far as I know this was always done at the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council. And if the Trial Chamber allows, I would like to add that in my capacity as the accused, I was able to see the evidence -- the fifth session of the Supreme Defence Council from the month of June in 1998, when General Perisic, the chief of the General Staff, proposed in June that the president of the state should issue an ordinance appointing me to this post that under the establishment was supposed to be held by a general, and I had already performed that duty for six months, and on the 25th of December, 1998, again at the session of the Supreme Defence Council, the then chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, proposed to President Milosevic and to the entire Supreme Defence Council that I be appointed to the duty of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the proposal is made by the chief of the General Staff, and then it goes up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is the procedure that could be seen both from the evidence and it could be also observed in practice, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, your reference to the month of June 1998 and the proposal of Perisic, what post were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the post of the chief of Staff of the Nis Corps that I had been in for six months by that time, but that was on the order of the chief of the General Staff, not according to the ordinance of the president, and this was something that had -- was supposed to be done as early as at the beginning of the year. So, in fact, that was the chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to complete with this. This will be my last-but-one question on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that the commendations are entered into the personnel file?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the personnel file is a Defence exhibit. It bears the number 5D1326. And we don't have to open it because it does not have a translation, but we would like to mark it for identification, and all these things that the general noted regarding the commendations and awards can be seen in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, when did your professional military service cease?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My professional military career ended on the 5th of October, 2004, at my personal request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I go back to the personnel file, please. How big is this file?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the personnel file has nine pages. At least that's what it says in the forms here. And the written commendations are entered in paragraph 15, which is entitled "Commendations and Awards."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, let us move in chronological order, but quite quickly, through the year 1998. Right at the beginning, I would like to know whether the military doctrine, the military rules and the Rules of Service, envisaged the use of the military against a kind of terrorism, armed rebellion, or against terrorist and rebel actions.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about some rules that dated from the 1970s or mid-1980s, from that earlier period, but from the 1990 onwards, as you said, the military doctrine and the Rules of Combat, in particular the Rules of Service in the Army of Yugoslavia, envisage and demand the involvement of the military in the fight against sabotage, terrorist, renegade, rebel, revolutionary forces. There is a number of terms that are used in the Rules of Combat and Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, based on your experience in the field, how were the terrorist forces organised, the rebel forces in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, what were their goals?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 are a classic example of an illegal paramilitary force whose goal was to subvert the constitutional order and to perpetrate systematic violence against individuals and the authority of the state. And we should not delve too deep into history, but the secessionist goals had been proclaimed a lot earlier. Their goal was to establish an ethnically-pure, independent state in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court Prosecution Exhibit P2453, and I would like you to comment on it, to comment on the situation that the Pristina Corps faced as early as 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, this is a working meeting of the staffs of Glogan, Duskaja, Baran Valley and Drin Valley. The date is the 23rd of June, 1998. Could we please zoom in. And could you please read, on the first page, the last paragraph from where it says the linking of the strategic axes in the Junik area.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He went on to talk about the geo-strategic significance of the zone of Dukadjin for us and for the enemy, the fact that our supply lines go through this zone where the border is and the enemy supply lines are, linking up the strategic operations axis in the Junicko Polje, and the other parts of Dukadjin is a precondition for the expansion of the war, for supplying the parts that cannot yet be supplied, and this leads to the ultimate liberation of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can you comment on this? What is this area? This will be important for us. It will help us understand better some of the testimony regarding Meja.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document from the so-called General Staff of the KLA. It was presented to the Trial Chamber and to all of us through Mr. Zyrapi, a Prosecution witness. What I've just read pertains to the territory of Metohija between Djakovica and Decani. This is a strategically important part of the border area where the armed rebellion in 1998 assumed frightening proportions, I would say, and members and leaders of the terrorist forces in this area are discussing this. The first person has been identified, that's Ramush Haradinaj, as Mr. Zyrapi testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We will go into that, General, afterwards, who testified to what, but in order to move forwards a bit quicker, could you please just comment about what area it is? Or, rather, now I would like us to move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you asked about a doctrine and rules which envisaged the use of the military in anti-terrorist activity. Are you going to be directing our attention to any of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will move on to that a little bit later. What we want to do now is -- in fact, we started with the first topic, the personnel file, and now what we want to do is we want to paint a picture for the Trial Chamber of what the Pristina Corps faced in 1998, and then we want to move on specifically to the way it was used, legitimate, unlegitimate, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General -- in fact, I would like to scroll down this page a little bit. The last sentence at the end of this page, where it says "Smajl," could you please read it and comment on it, just this one sentence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, "Smajl": "To assist one another in the future, we have to supply weapons to the whole population from the age of 16 up." My comment -- or rather this is something that I was personally aware of, because I was at the forward command post in Djakovica at that time and I was able to monitor all those developments. I experienced this on my own skin. I survived it. In June, the armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija spread to the Djakovica and Decani municipalities, in particularly the Reka e Keqe area, the Caragoj valley, Junicko Polje because this was the shortest corridor that the terrorist forces could use to ship in huge amounts of personnel and weapons from Albania, and this sentence shows that there was a mobilisation, and I know that for a fact. It was a forced mobilisation carried out by the organisers of the armed rebellion. They mobilised children aged 16. And if the Trial Chamber allows me to explain why I know that, I know that because those villages were, for the most part, Catholic villages, and they applied to the military and to the Minister of Interior. They wanted us to protect them. They didn't want to take up those weapons, and they didn't want to side with the armed rebellion against the authorities and the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: According to your operational intelligence, what strength were the forces of the KLA or the armed rebel forces in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The armed rebellion escalated in July 1998. At that time, what you say is correct, the operational intelligence, but it turned out that these were actual facts. They speak about between 20.000 and 25.000 armed rebels in the so-called operational component. This is the rapid reaction force, so to speak. They had tactical units and all the way up to operational zones. And as for the strength of the local -- the territorial component in the villages, it is difficult to speak of it. To my knowledge, there were several tens of thousands of people who were involved in the armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please move to Exhibit 5D1307. This is an operations report -- this is a report of the security sector of the Pristina Corps of the 24th of July, 1998. You can see here in the first paragraph an assessment of the numerical strength, and I should like to ask you to just briefly comment on the actual nuclei and the places where this armed rebellion was the most massive, which will be of relevance for us to assist the crime base from the indictment. I'm saying this in order to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the importance of this comment.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the security organ of the Pristina Corps, addressed to the Security Administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to the Security Department of the 3rd Army and to the organ of security of the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, as we do not have the translation, please just read the first paragraph and let us end it there.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So finish this sentence. You said the Counter-Intelligence Group --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Counter-Intelligence Group, and this speaks about the numerical strength and the concentration of the terrorist forces of the armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm going to read a few sentences which describe this: "The available intelligence indicates that currently in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, there are 25.000 armed terrorists involved in terrorist groupations. The corps of the terrorist groups are located in the general area of the Drenica, Malisevo, Glodjan, Jablanica and Junik. Currently, the terrorists are controlling around 50 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to stop you there. I see Mr. Hannis is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to know, Your Honour -- this is another one for which we do not have a translation, and this one is more problematic for me. I hope I'll have a translation before I have to start cross-examination of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's a question of seeking relief as required. We know that this one is not translated, from looking at the screen. You don't need to intervene each time. We'll allow you, obviously, to have whatever relief you require to deal adequately with these when it comes to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, with that advice, Your Honour, then I won't pop up every time, but I felt it was necessary to point out on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've prepared myself to give just two short indications and then move on to the end of the text, which shows the stamp, which can confirm the authenticity of this document. There is no signature, but the stamp corroborates its authenticity. Perhaps that can be of assistance to colleague Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can we move on to the second page. And in order to progress as fast as possible, just tell me, General, in paragraph 4, what place is referred to as a terrorist place in Kosovo, as a terrorist stronghold, in fact?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, there is reference to the village of Junik, and it gives the actual specific names of the people in question, as well as the villages of Smonica and Nivokaz. This is towards Djakovica and the Caragoj Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're waiting for the interpretation. Your Honour, there is an important mistake in the interpretation, because -- and it is important because of the crime base and the incidents that we have been dealing with for a year and a half. What it should read, it should read the village of Smonica and the valley of Caragoj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in the penultimate paragraph on this same page, is there any reference to the existence of reliable data to the effect that in the village of Ramoc, there are 63 armed terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. In the village of Ramoc, which is in Caragoj valley, there was detected a group numbering 63 armed terrorists headed by a man from the Niki [phoen] Family. You didn't ask me about the rest of it, but what it says, with leave from the Trial Chamber, is also confirmation of what I've already said, which is that the villages -- the locals from that part of Metohija, from the village of Korenica, refused to take up arms and asked the MUP and the army to help them not be forcibly armed by the insurgent forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is important for us to stress the reference to the village of Ramoc because it is also referred to in the testimony of Nike Peraj and in the Prosecution witness K73's testimony, and so that's why we feel we need to put particular stress on this. I should now like us to see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And please comment on the stamp on the last page, in terms of its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This document was sent as a telegram, by what are called "cryptographic protected communication links." That is why there is no signature, and this stamp is the stamp which is used at the cryptographic processing station, indicating when it was received and when it had been sent. We saw in the heading to whom it had been sent, and this here is proof that that telegram was indeed received at that particular hour, minute, and on that particular date, or actually sent to the addresses which are indicated in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We went through some pieces of evidence. I should like to hear your operational assessment and assessment from what your experience on the ground, what was the tactic applied by the KLA in order to achieve their aims in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was a classical terrorist and paramilitary tactic, which is also familiar, unfortunately, in other countries. In Kosovo and Metohija, there were two elaborated components of that tactic. The first one was widespread action throughout the province, predominantly targeting rural areas, the so-called "1.000 fires" tactics, and the second tactic, which is quite inhumane but is classical and is associated with terrorism, is the "two villages" tactic. And with permission from the Trial Chamber, I should like to clarify the second tactic. What that means is that one village is evacuated of civilians, and it then constitutes a fortified military territory stronghold from which attacks are launched on the forces and authorities of the state and civilians and citizens and individuals, whereas in the second village is concentrated the civilian population which extends logistical and other support, but which is extremely inhumane, is also a live shield, a human shield for the terrorist forces when they clash with the security forces and it serves the civilian population that is, and is used and abused to simulate different humanitarian and other crises, and projecting an impression to the effect that the security forces are attacking peaceful Albanian villages and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the command of the 3rd Army, or, rather, first of all the Pristina Corps and then the Command of the 3rd Army to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia send such reports about such an assessment of the situation, I mean, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Reports were sent daily, not only assessments. I should say factual figures, data about all these things, including the forward command post in Djakovica, to the Pristina Corps, to the 3rd Army Command and to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what is the "thousand fires" tactic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished Presiding Judge, I have abridged my answer in order not to invoke the ideological programmes of the KLA which actually define this tactic, and it presupposes -- it implies that throughout the area of Kosovo and Metohija, there must be an armed insurgency, an armed rebellion as they put it, against Serbia. "A thousand fires," this is Mao Zedong's theory, in fact. That is, that every cell, every village, every settlement, should have a cell of a paramilitary, or even a paramilitary unit which would undertake operations measures against the state of Serbia and its institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My last question had to do with the reports, and in order for us to move on quickly, I should like to draw the Chamber's attention to Exhibits number 5D56 and 5D55.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did there exist orders to evacuate -- to move out civilians at that time by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We, in the Pristina Corps, had concrete information and facts to the effect that within this overall tactic, and I should state "strategy," the leadership of the armed rebellion was actually provoking the re-settlement and migration of the civilian population from areas where they planned to later attack security forces or they moved them out in order to simulate a humanitarian crisis. Such reports were submitted practically daily, and they were numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court Exhibit 5D1298, and this, Your Honours, is also an exhibit that we don't have a translation of, and I should like it to be marked for identification. This is a telegram by Mr. Lazarevic which he can briefly comment on, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, any document which has not been translated will automatically be marked for identification. You referred a moment ago to 5D56 and 5D55. What are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are combat reports, and I should just like to refer the Court to them because we do not want Mr. Lazarevic to amplify on the subject. These are 5D55 -- this is a combat report of the 3rd Army of the 26 -- of the 12 of July, 1998, and the second one is a report of the 11th of May, 1998, also a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you are required to do is include these in motions for admission of documents from the Bar table and explain how they were put in context in the evidence. And as long as we know that that's going to happen, then we don't need to take up time exploring them in the oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was precisely my intention, but of course I await instructions from you. All the exhibits that we do not open and do not comment with the general shall be put on the list, and we shall ask for them to be tendered as you have instructed. But perhaps -- I thought it was perhaps convenient to refer the Trial Chamber to the exhibit in question in the transcript in order to establish the appropriate link, but if you do not feel that that is appropriate, I shall refrain from doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it is very helpful to do that and just add a word to explain that these are both combat reports. That would have completed the picture. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is my mistake. Mr. Hannis referred to 600 exhibits, and how that sounded discouraging, and if we were to have all of those, the trial would actually last until the December recess. That is why we want to move through some of the exhibits in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please comment on this, what I believe to be a telegram, and it indicates it is by you. Do you recognise this, or, rather, do you know what this is? It is dated the 15th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I certainly know what this is. The Command of the Pristina Corps, the forward command post at which I was for most of 1998, and the signature indicates my name and surname and my duty. Of course, there is no signature because it is a telegram. I am submitting information to a part of the units in Metohija. And as far as I understood you, you want me to comment on the last paragraph, namely, that terrorists ordered -- or should I read it, perhaps. "In Djakovica, two women and children from Djakovica --" Rather: "Women and children from Djakovica were ordered to move out because in the forthcoming several days an attack on Djakovica is expected." And the moving out is in Kos. In the last sentence, I asked a number of units to assess the situation and to undertake the necessary measures in order -- given the announced attacks. If I need to say anything more in connection with this, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, thank you. We shall move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The absence of translation may be a problem here. It's not clear to me who's being ordered by whom, from what you've said so far, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the first sentence it says that I, as regards this information on the intentions and actions of the forces of the armed rebellion in the area of Djakovica, that I received this information from the intelligence subcentre in Pristina. That is an intelligence structure which is part of the army, and it's subordinated to the 3rd Army. They said that there would be an attack on the town of Djakovica, that civilians were being moved out of Djakovica, and I am warning the Military Police Battalion, the 52nd Artillery Brigade, the 53rd mortar Battalion and Combat Group 52 which were in the general area of Djakovica, that they should take a note of the situation and that they should take measures to prevent any surprises, they should take protection measures in case there was a terrorist attack on the forces of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But who was expected to attack Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terrorist forces would attack the Djakovica garrison. They would also attack the MUP forces, the forces of the Secretariat of the Interior, and other institutions also. But in this document, I'm referring primarily to the army and warning the units which are in Djakovica and its general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this points out the problem that I'm having with the untranslated documents, because in his earlier answer, at page 30, line 12, he said, and it's in quotes -- I'm sorry, line 14: "Women and children from Djakovica were ordered to move out." It doesn't say by whom. In his later answer at page 31, line 5 or 6, he says: "They said that there would be an attack on a town Djakovica, that the civilians were being moved out." It's important to know whether they were ordered and by whom, and I can't tell from this what it says, and that's why the translation is important. And if there's going to be a motion to admit several of the documents on the list in a written filing after the General's done, and those are documents that weren't translated while he was still here for me to cross-examine, I have a problem and I may be requesting to recall him to cross-examine him about those documents that I didn't have translations for when he was on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty is noted. You'll appreciate we're also having difficulty with this, Mr. Hannis, but again I can only repeat we'll deal with the problem as and when it materialises. I think you make a good point, however, about the need for all documents to be available in translated form before the evidence of Mr. Lazarevic is completed. Mr. Bakrac, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will ask the members of my team to contact CLSS and ask them to translate these documents that we have used so far as soon as possible in order to make them available to Mr. Hannis and the Trial Chamber. Well, here is a document which has been translated for you to comment on. It's 3D1001. Could it be brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please read the third paragraph, where it says: "The women and children have fled from Junik ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram sent by the security organ of the Pristina Corps, dated the 1st of August, 1998, addressed to the Security Administration of the General Staff, and I quote: "The women and children have fled from Junik, as have a number of terrorists, a large number of terrorists, who have abandoned their weapons and gone to the Republic of Albania or into the interior. There are now about 700 terrorists in Junik."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, the date is the 1st of August, 1998. We will come to this very quickly. Is this within the scope of the Voksa-Slup Operation in Junik?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was taking place at the time, but it was not an operation, just some actions to neutralise the nuclei of the armed rebellion in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, from the evidence presented here, we may conclude that the border villages in the municipalities of Djakovica and Decani were, for the most part, the centres of armed rebellion, can you tell us whether you know what the reason for that was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I know about it is the following: This was a strategic area, the border area. From the military viewpoint, these were major strategic axes from Albania which might be used to infiltrate terrorist forces from Albania. And later on, as was shown in 1999, they could be also used for a ground force aggression. Secondly, the ethnic composition in that part of Metohija was practically 100 per cent Albanian. And, thirdly, in that area there were large numbers of people who had moved in from Albania, and these were Albanians who had never received Serbian citizenship or applied for Serbian citizenship, and they strengthened the rebellion in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, this may be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, you explained to us, before the break, about the reason why the villages in the border area were the nuclei of the rebellion. Would it be fair to say that by mid-1998 already, the security of the state border in fact turned into the defence of the state border, and what would be the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that securing the state border facing Albania on a front that is longer than 150 kilometres had been difficult even in the earlier period in April, as early as April. In fact, we were defending the state border. The difference between securing and defending the state border is the following, in brief: Securing the state border, in all countries of the world, is something that is done by the border units, the police and the military units, in accordance with the procedure that is envisaged, the peacetime procedure, and here we're talking about the classical defence against daily attacks launched from Albania. In 1998, those attacks numbered 500. The attacks would be in groups ranging in size from eight to ten people up to 800 armed terrorists from Albania, so that would be a classical form of an attempt to penetrate the state border. And the exhibit that we saw a little while ago spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now that we're talking about this topic, could we please comment on 5D1306, Exhibit 5D1306. It is one of the last exhibits that we intend to use that has not been translated yet, so could we please have 5D1306 in e-court, please. Because we don't have the translation, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what kind of a document is this and what is the date?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a report in the form of a telegram from the Security Department in the Pristina Corps Command, sent to the Security Administration in the General Staff and the Security Section of the 3rd Army, and the date is the 20th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to move on to the next page, and I would like you to read and comment very briefly on the first paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I quote: "During the day, the security organs of the Pristina Corps captured Femu Kokici [phoen], father's name Zek [phoen]" we have the personal details here. Together with 700 terrorists, he participated in an attempted to violently penetrate our territory in the Djerevica border post area in the night of the 17th and 18th of July, 1998. If the Trial Chamber allows, I can say that I was personally in that area at that time, and I experienced firsthand this classical act of aggression launched in peacetime from a neighbouring country involving this number of armed individuals. In the course of 1998, 9.000 people tried to penetrate the state border, and that would be the strength equivalent to a division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us move on now. I would like to know, after the agreement of the 13th of October, 1998, the Yugoslav Army troops withdrew to the barracks. What was the KLA response to this fact? Did it exploit it in any way, and if "yes," in what way, the fact that the VJ had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija disengaged in a single day. It was brought back into the barracks, with the exception of the units securing and defending the state border under disagreement. On the very same day, the terrorist forces throughout Kosovo and Metohija took the positions that had been held by the security forces. By that, I mean the forces of the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and the forces of the 3rd Army predominantly of the Pristina Corps, and the OSCE mission had not yet been established at that time. There was just a KDOM mission, the Kosovo Diplomatic Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally we have an exhibit that has a translation, so could we please comment on 5D95. Could we please have it brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, we're waiting for the English translation, but while we do that, perhaps you could just confirm, to speed things up, this is a regular combat report of the 3rd Army Command, dated the 15th of October, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is a combat report sent to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2, paragraph 4, the last passage, and could you please comment on it. It continues on to the third page. Could you just read it and comment on it, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could I have paragraph 1 -- paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please just read the first sentence in the second passage?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I see here on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can't see the beginning of the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom out- we don't need to have it so big- so we can see the beginning of the paragraph? Could you scroll down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Okay, here you see it, paragraph 4, the first sentence therein.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic reports to the chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, that on the 15th of October, 1998, there was a huge concentration of the terrorist forces, about 3.000 of them, in the municipality of Podujevo, along the Pristina-Podujevo-Nis main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We're talking -- while we're on the topic of this road, was this the main route leading to the rest of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, leading to Serbia from -- linking the province with Serbia, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the second passage, it says here in this report that the terrorists have fortified their positions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, this sentence contains my explanation of the tactics employed in two villages. Villages would be fortified as classical strongholds, and attacks were launched from those strongholds against the institutions of the state. The Mijanca [phoen] village is in the immediate vicinity of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, finally, the last passage in here -- I apologise. I warned you not to talk too fast, and now I'm doing that mistake. Sir, could you please look at the last passage on the same page, and could you please just comment on it? It begins with the words: "On the 15th of October at 1715 hours ...," right at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it. In this report, the 3rd Army commander states that there was a terrorist attack against a group of vehicles from the 125th Motorised Brigade in the Volujak-Klina-Mitrovica Axis, and Volujak is the place that was stipulated in the agreement, that there could be a mixed company stationed there in accordance with the agreement that envisaged the disengagement of all the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the agreement was signed on the 13th, and this group of the 125th Brigade was in a location where it was supposed to be under the agreement, yet an attack was launched a bare two days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and in the previous passage we read that an attack was launched on the Stari Trg road. Well, I don't want to go into all that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us now move on. After the agreement and after the arrival of the foreign observers and verifiers, did the Army of Yugoslavia carry out any preparations for a so-called "spring offensive" or anything of the sort? So I'm talking -- I'm asking you about the Army of Yugoslavia, because you were at the time the chief of Staff in the Corps, you were in the field. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to state the following: This is contained in a report signed by me, sent from a forward command post to the Corps Command in Pristina, stating that the members of the corps units that secured and defended the state border welcomed this agreement with a great deal of good faith, hoping that it would end the armed rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija and in a -- within the space of a sigle day, and this is quite a military feat. I participated in it myself. All the units disengaged, including the units that had fortified -- that had reinforced the Pristina Corps, they left -- these units left the province, and 60 per cent of all the corps units went back to their peacetime garrisons, carrying out their regular duties. Even if any such desire existed, this kind of operation could not be taken as any preparation for an offensive, but preparation for a peacetime functioning in a situation where we have the verification mission coming in. So to my knowledge, there were no activities, no plans, at least as far as the Pristina Corps is concerned, existed, and I think this holds true for the entire army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did you have any information that the KLA, following the withdrawal of the army and the arrival of the foreign verifiers, was in fact preparing for a spring offensive?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not only did we have operational intelligence, as you call it, but the situation in the overall territory of Kosovo and Metohija escalated, in terms of posing a risk to the lives of the civilians, the military, the MUP and the state institutions. We did have some dates -- some operational intelligence about the dates when the armed rebellion would be relaunched, but in new conditions in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm talking about the facts. From day to day, the number of attacks in Kosovo and Metohija grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D1035 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us what this is? Who issued this document, what is the date?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram from the Pristina Corps Command, the Security Department. It is sent to the Security Administration and General Staff, the 3rd Army Security Section, the 14th Counter-Intelligence Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on it and read just the second paragraph? Or, rather, we have paragraph 1: "Situation at the border," and then the last sentence in the second paragraph, beginning with the words: "In Tropoja" do you find that: "In Tropoja the KLA members ..."?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Members of the KLA were told that they were to be trained for a broader -- for broader combat operations that were to take place in the spring of 1999 in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. If it's necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I wanted you just to finish. The commander of the staff in Tropoja?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Staff in Tropoja was Agram Rahman [phoen] from a village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- near Djakovica. This is what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did you have any other information other intelligence that a spring offensive was in the making, apart from such reports to the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to stress that this information was obtained from the members of those paramilitary forces. This man had been in Albania. He had been trained there, and he had been given this task. But quite naturally, we had other reports to rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should stop you here, and we will bring this topic to a close. Could we please have 3D1038 brought up in e-court, please. We're waiting for the translation. Could you please read the first sentence, or, rather, the first sentence in 2(1), paragraph 2(1) on page 1, and could you explain to us what it means, "electronic reconnaissance"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a document again from the Security Section of the Pristina Corps Command. The date is the 29th of December. It is five days later than the previous one. And I quote: "Information was obtained through the application of electronic reconnaissance indicating that there were intensive preparations of terrorists for a spring offensive in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Fleeing from forced mobilisation, Siptars are increasingly moving out of Kosovo and Metohija via Montenegro to the Republic of Albania and then to EU countries." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, this is enough.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You asked me to explain what electronic reconnaissance measures are. In 1998, in the Pristina Corps, there were establishment units that were tasked with electronic reconnaissance, and the focus of their activities was to monitor the armed rebellion forces in Kosovo and Metohija and the area around it, and the corps was reinforced by a special unit from the 3rd Army. That was the Electronic Reconnaissance Unit that was used to monitor the so-called Sabotage Unit communications. So this was a respectable force that was able to carry out audio surveillance and to intercept the flow of information among the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And let us now close with this topic of the spring offensive. I will now show you a short video clip, about a minute and a half, and maybe you can confirm whether you did have this kind of information. This is a BBC video clip that's Exhibit 5D1241. Could we please have it played.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "[Indiscernible] If a peace deal is going to be so, this is going to be one of the hardest places to sell it. [Indiscernible] They say they trust nothing but their guns, and they will surrender them only to the government of an independent Kosovo. [Indiscernible] BBC News, [indiscernible] in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my team has an intervention. It was a poor -- what is missing in the transcript is that they were preparing themselves for war and not for peace. Perhaps someone could listen to the tape and rectify it in the transcript. Rather, it would be more expedient than have us go through the film again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly heard that on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've dealt with it adequately. What it didn't tell us is where it was, and who they were, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we heard this from the reporter, that it was in Kosovo. I was just about to ask the General whether he recognised, by their uniforms, who these people were, and perhaps he also recognised the place. So I'm going to ask the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can you recognise, on the basis of the uniforms, who these men were?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can recognise the location. I do recognise the location quite reliably. That is the Mountain Drenica, or "Berisa" as they called it in Kosovo and Metohija, and a notorious place called "Klecka," a crematorium in the 20th century that I know of for civilians used by the terrorist forces. On the 29th of January, 1999, in that village -- this was recorded in that village, and one can see that it is empty. This is the "two villages" tactic. This is a completely evacuated village which is a terrorist stronghold, and there is no doubt at all that this is a paramilitary unit of a company rank in this village. Unfortunately, they are wearing Yugoslav Army uniforms, but they have the UCK or the KLA patches. But I know about events and from events in that period, where they were, and there is no doubt whatsoever that this was the location where a terrorist group was located on this Berisa Mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we also saw a woman in civilian clothes with a heavy machine-gun -- with a machine-gun. Was this a frequent occurrence? Did you see men and women, civilians, wearing uniform -- bearing arms and belonging to such units?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a large amount of information corroborating that there were men and women and children that were given weapons or had taken up arms, and we had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, can we conclude that despite the presence of the OSCE mission, Albanian villages kept being transformed into bases, and the KLA prepare there for a spring offensive? Was there a large number of such places where they -- was this practice widespread?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the Corps Command and the 3rd Army Command, we had verified data on villages in which there were located large groups of terrorist forces and of the armed rebellion forces. There were between 400 and 600 such villages where there were at all times the terrorist forces and the insurgent forces throughout Kosovo and Metohija. So to directly answer your question, I would say, yes, Albanian villages, after September and October, were again in large numbers converted into terrorist strongholds and classical military bases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I think the date may have been the 22nd of January, rather than the 29th. This was a television broadcast, it would appear. Were you aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had ample evidence, actually our own recordings, but we did not mount any attacks on such strongholds during the OSCE mission. We did have video materials that we were given by journalists or that we obtained by way of intelligence cooperation with certain structures on the ground. What I said in relation to this was that I recognised the location, the surroundings. I know the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're trying to anticipate what I want to know, and it would be better if you just answered my question. Were you aware of this television broadcast at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My reason for asking was if this sort of conduct, which you say is contrary to the agreement, was being so blatantly undertaken by terrorists, what were you, as by then the head of the Pristina Corps, doing about it? You were taking no action, as you say. Were you not communicating with the KVM about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, what I said was we did not attack these strongholds, and I offered no further explanation, but now I'm going to respond to your question. The daily meetings of teams of the 3rd Army and of the Pristina Corps with the OSCE mission in Pristina were, inter alia, used to draw attention to these occurrences, and I can also add that the OSCE mission itself very often informed us with concern about what was happening on the ground, what was being done by KLA members, in other words, where they were fortifying themselves and what they were preparing for the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that somebody in the VJ would be monitoring television broadcasts of this nature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you that it was probably so, and with your permission I should like to add the following: In order to be precise, from Ms. or Mrs. Sally Baker, who was accused for illegally crossing the state border from Albania, we had obtained voluminous material which was recorded in this way in Smonica and Djakovica, and we sent it to the Security Administration, and this is a specific example that I should like to draw your attention to. This was voluminous material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I believe part of the answer is not recorded. I believe the witness said it was shown to the OSCE as well. It was sent to the Security Administration of the Command Staff of the VJ Army and at the same time was shown to the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that we sent the video materials and the documentation on the activities of the forces of the armed rebellion by regular channels to the 3rd Army, the Security Administration and the 3rd Army, and that we also sent it to the OSCE, that we actually familiarised the mission, the OSCE mission, with activities on the ground being carried out by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let us wrap up this topic. And in order for us to do so, please be so kind as to comment. Exhibit 5D1334. I might have misspoken. 5D1334. We're waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But will you read this out so we won't need the translation? What is this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a survey of armed Albanian villages in Kosovo and Metohija- terrorist basis- in 1998 and 1999. This a so-called "survey map" which shows not all the terrorist bases but basically the main groupings of the armed rebellion forces in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please not overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, these blue points mark that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the rectangles mark in yellow and green colour the settlements in the different municipalities, their number, and how many of those settlements have been converted into terrorist strongholds, but it is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Of course, this can be analysed subsequently. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, on this map, at the top, there is a heading and a subheading. Do you know who prepared this map and whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map which was made in the operations organ together with the security organ of the Pristina Corps, that is.
